title: Checkpoint: Shooting a Scene
objective: After this level you can explain how planning, crew, camera and light work together to capture a single scene.
summary: The clapperboard labels each take and marks one instant on picture and sound. The chapter traced a scene from script and plan to crew, camera and light.

cards.headline: Chapter 3 finale: every take begins with a snap.
cards.body: Just before a take, someone holds a board up in the camera's view and claps it shut. That small ritual ties together the plan, the crew and the camera from this whole chapter. Here's what it does, then the chapter in one breath.

cards.headline: The clapper: a label and a sound
cards.body: Britannica describes the clapper, or clapperboard: a slate showing information about the take, topped by a hinged arm. Its wooden jaws, about a foot long, are snapped together in the picture, so the moment of the clack is recorded on both the picture and the sound. When sound and picture are recorded separately, editors use that shared cue to match them.

mascot.line: It connects: the slate numbers on this board are what Level 24's script supervisor writes down, take after take.

cards.headline: The whole chapter in one scene
cards.body: A film moves through development, pre-production, filming, post-production and distribution. On paper, each screenplay page is about a minute, and storyboards and shot lists plan every shot. On set, the cinematographer shoots each scene for the director and decides how the camera moves; depth of field decides what's sharp; the gaffer's lights set the mood, high-key or low-key.

cards.headline: Chapter 3 complete
learned: How a film travels from idea to audience in five stages, and who does what on set.
Why a screenplay page counts as about a minute, and how storyboards and shot lists plan shots.
How shot size, camera angle and camera movement change what you notice and feel.
How lenses, focus and three-point lighting decide what's sharp and set a scene's mood.

questions.prompt: What does a clapperboard's slate show?

options.label: The screenplay's page count for the scene
options.rationale: Page count estimates running time; the slate labels the take.

options.label: Information about the take being filmed
The gaffer's lighting plan
options.rationale: The lighting scheme isn't written on the slate.

options.label: The film's budget
options.rationale: Budgets belong to the producer, not the slate.

questions.explanation: The slate carries information about the take, and its hinged arm claps down to mark the start.

questions.prompt: How does the clapper's snap help editors line up sound and picture that were recorded separately?

options.label: It switches the camera and the sound recorder on together
options.rationale: It doesn't control the equipment; it marks a moment.

options.label: It tells the actors exactly when to speak
options.rationale: Its job is marking picture and sound, not cueing lines.

options.label: The clack lands on both recordings at the same instant
It records which lens the camera is using
options.rationale: Lens notes are the script supervisor's job.

questions.explanation: The jaws snap shut in the picture, and the clack is recorded on the sound, so editors match that one instant.

questions.prompt: Match each piece of filmmaking with what it does, from script to set.
questions.explanation: Each screenplay page is about a minute, depth of field decides what's sharp, the gaffer's lights set the mood, and the clapper's slate shows information about the take.

questions.prompt: A camera placed well below eye level, looking up, tends to make a character seem what?

options.label: Small and weak
options.rationale: That's the usual effect of a high angle.

options.label: Uneasy and off balance
options.rationale: That's the effect of a Dutch angle.

options.label: Far away and tiny in the landscape
options.rationale: That's a long shot, a question of size.

questions.explanation: A low angle can make a character look heroic and strong or, for a villain, intimidating.

questions.prompt: A horror scene needs shadows hiding half a face and a sense that something is wrong. Which pair of choices fits?

options.label: High-key lighting and an eye-level shot
options.rationale: High-key is bright with few shadows, and eye level feels natural.

options.label: Low-key lighting and a Dutch angle
High-key lighting and a wide establishing shot
options.rationale: That gives a bright, clear view of where we are.

options.label: A strong fill light and a medium shot
options.rationale: More fill softens shadows instead of deepening them.

questions.explanation: Low-key lighting leaves deep shadows, and a Dutch angle's tilted frame suggests that something isn't right.
